hints: Start by counting carbons. Pyruvate is a 3-carbon molecule and the acetyl group is 2-carbon, so what small carbon-containing molecule must have been lost?
Think about what happens to hydrogen in this step. NAD is converted to NADH here, so what name is given to removal of hydrogen, which is also a type of oxidation?
walkthrough:
Follow the carbons to spot decarboxylation**
Pyruvate has 3 carbons and the acetyl group has only 2 carbons. That missing carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. Whenever $CO_2$ is removed from a molecule we call it decarboxylation.

Follow the hydrogens to spot oxidation**
At the same time hydrogen is removed from pyruvate and picked up by NAD to make NADH + $H^+$. Removal of hydrogen is called dehydrogenation, and because loss of hydrogen is loss of electrons, it is also oxidation.
Final answer: Decarboxylation - removal of carbon dioxide from pyruvate; dehydrogenation / oxidation - removal of hydrogen from pyruvate.

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 8.1. At any one concentration of acetyl-coA, compare the height of the without succinyl-coA curve with the with succinyl-coA curve. What is the overall effect?
Pick one acetyl-coA concentration, for example 60 or 80, and read off the two activity values. How does quoting numbers strengthen your description?
You are told acetyl-coA and succinyl-coA have a similar shape. Think about what similar-shaped molecules do at an enzyme active site and how they compete.
Succinyl-coA is made later in the Krebs cycle but acts on the first enzyme. Think about why slowing the first step when a later product builds up is useful control.
walkthrough:
Describe what the graph shows**
For every concentration of acetyl-coA, activity is lower with succinyl-coA present. For example, at 60 arbitrary units of acetyl-coA, activity is about 0.70 without succinyl-coA but only about 0.25 with succinyl-coA. At 80 units it is about 0.85 without but only about 0.44 with. So succinyl-coA clearly inhibits citrate synthase.

Explain the type of inhibition**
Acetyl-coA is the substrate for citrate synthase. Because succinyl-coA has a similar shape, it can fit into the same active site and block acetyl-coA from binding. That is competitive inhibition. More acetyl-coA can out-compete it, which is why activity still rises at very high substrate concentration.

Link to regulation of the cycle**
Succinyl-coA is produced later in the Krebs cycle. If it accumulates, it slows the first step catalysed by citrate synthase. This slows the whole cycle and stops excess citrate and other intermediates being made. It is a form of feedback / end-product inhibition that matches cycle rate to need.

Final answer: Succinyl-coA reduces activity of citrate synthase, e.g. at 60 acetyl-coA activity is approx. 0.70 without and approx. 0.25 with succinyl-coA; succinyl-coA binds to the active site of citrate synthase as a competitive inhibitor; this slows the Krebs cycle and prevents build-up of citrate / intermediates.

hints: Focus only on stages inside the mitochondrion. Which two stages release hydrogen from substrates and need a carrier to pick it up?
Think about what NAD becomes when it picks up that hydrogen, and what word we use for a molecule that carries hydrogen between stages.
Follow where that reduced carrier goes next inside the mitochondrion. Which membrane structure is the site of the electron transport chain?
Think about what must happen to the carrier after it drops off its hydrogen so it can be used again.
walkthrough:
Pick up hydrogen in the matrix**
In the mitochondrial matrix, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle remove hydrogen from substrates by dehydrogenation / oxidation. NAD picks up this hydrogen and is reduced to NADH. So NAD is the hydrogen carrier that collects energy-rich hydrogen.

Deliver hydrogen to the cristae**
NADH then diffuses to the inner mitochondrial membrane / cristae. There it releases its hydrogen as protons and electrons to the electron transport chain for oxidative phosphorylation, where most ATP is made by chemiosmosis.

Recycle for continuous respiration**
After releasing hydrogen, NADH is oxidised back to NAD. This regeneration is vital because without a fresh supply of NAD, the link reaction and Krebs cycle would stop for lack of hydrogen acceptor.

Final answer: NAD acts as a hydrogen carrier, reduced to NADH in the link reaction and Krebs cycle; NADH moves to the inner mitochondrial membrane / cristae and releases hydrogen / protons and electrons for oxidative phosphorylation; NAD is oxidised / regenerated for reuse.
